title: From "Are We Compliant?" to a Signed Scope
description: Turn Havenmark's vague first email into a defined page sample, test matrix, deliverable list, and a price you can actually stand behind on a bad week.

learningObjectives.text: Convert a vague client request into a defined page sample, test matrix, deliverable list, and timeline
Price an accessibility audit by deliverable and calendar time rather than by promised hours

contentSections.body:
An email arrives from Marijke, Head of Digital at Havenmark, a mid-size home-and-lifestyle retailer trading across the EU out of Rotterdam:

> "Hi — we got a letter from one of our B2B buyers (a municipal library system) referencing the European Accessibility Act and asking us to confirm our webshop is compliant. We've never had an audit done. Can you tell us if we're okay? How much would this cost and how fast can you turn it around — we'd like this sorted before our next board meeting in three weeks."

This is a real, paying opportunity, and it is also almost useless as a brief. "Tell us if we're okay" isn't a scope. "How fast" isn't a timeline. If you quote against this email as written, you are quoting against a moving target you defined for the client instead of one they agreed to — and the first time your findings surprise them, or your invoice does, that gap is where the relationship breaks.

A scope statement turns "audit our site" into four things a client can read, agree to, and hold you to — and that you can hold *them* to when the request changes later.

**The page sample.** Not "the whole site" — a defined, representative set of templates. A retail site like Havenmark's repeats the same handful of templates across hundreds of URLs, so auditing every product page tells you nothing that auditing three doesn't. A defensible sample covers every *distinct* interaction pattern once: homepage, category/listing page, product detail page, search results (including zero-results), cart, checkout (each distinct step), account creation and login, and at least one content-heavy form (contact, returns, or newsletter signup). That is a sample, not a shortcut — a finding on the product-detail template is a finding on every page that uses it, which is exactly why sampling one page per template is honest, not lazy.

**The test matrix.** Which standard, which success criteria, which assistive technology combinations. For an EU retailer under EAA pressure, that's WCAG 2.1 Level AA (the standard EN 301 549 points to) tested with at minimum: keyboard-only navigation, one screen reader/browser pairing per major OS (NVDA + Chrome, VoiceOver + Safari), 200% browser zoom, and a spot check with voice control on any custom interactive component. Naming the matrix up front stops a later "but did you check on Firefox" from becoming free scope.

**The deliverables.** What the client actually receives: a written audit report with findings rated by severity, an executive summary a non-technical stakeholder can read in five minutes, and — named separately, because it costs separately — a live or recorded walkthrough of the findings.

**The timeline**, stated in calendar weeks, not hours worked. That distinction is the subject of the rest of this lesson.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's webshop has roughly 40 distinct page templates once you count every listing variant, filter state, and checkout step across their five country storefronts.
contentSections.question: Before reading on: how many pages belong in a defensible sample for the first audit?

options.label: 3–5 pages
8–12 pages
20–25 pages
All 40 templates

contentSections.revealBody: 8–12. That covers homepage, category listing, product detail, search (with a zero-results case), cart, two or three checkout steps, account/login, and one content form — one instance of every genuinely distinct interaction pattern. Three to five misses whole categories of interaction (nobody tested checkout). Twenty to twenty-five and all forty both re-test the same templates under different URLs — thoroughness in appearance, not in substance, and a timeline that can't survive a bad week because there was never a reason for it to be that long.

contentSections.body:
**Pricing this honestly starts with what you refuse to promise.** You cannot promise Havenmark forty hours of work across the next three weeks, because you don't know in advance how many of those weeks will be full-capacity ones. Promising hours is promising something outside your control, and breaking that promise on a bad week reads to a client as unreliability — even though the actual cause was never something a stronger work ethic would have fixed.

What you can promise is a **deliverable**, by a **date**, for a **fixed fee**. "A full audit report covering the agreed page sample, delivered within three weeks, for €X" is a promise about output and calendar time — both of which you control by how you plan the work, not by how many spoons a given Tuesday hands you. Whether you do the testing in four long sessions or twelve short ones is invisible to the client and irrelevant to the deliverable.

Two more things make a fixed-scope quote survivable:

**Build a buffer week into the stated timeline before the client sees it**, not after you're behind. If the honest estimate is two weeks of testing and writing, quote three. That week isn't slack you're hiding — it's the difference between a deadline that assumes every day is a good day and one that doesn't.

**State a response-time expectation, not an availability one.** "I reply to emails within two business days and hold walkthrough calls by scheduled appointment only" is a commitment you can keep on a bad week, because it says nothing about how many hours you worked that day — only about when the client hears back. "I'm available whenever you need me" is a commitment you cannot keep on a bad week, and having made it, a bad week now looks like a broken promise instead of what it actually is.

contentSections.scenario:
Two ways Marijke's email could be answered:

**Quote A:** "I bill at €75/hour. A full audit typically runs 30–40 hours, so budget €2,250–3,000. I'll start Monday and let you know how it's going."

**Quote B:** "A full audit of an 8–12 page representative sample — homepage through checkout, account, and one form — tested against WCAG 2.1 AA with NVDA, VoiceOver, keyboard-only, and 200% zoom, delivered as a severity-rated report plus a recorded findings walkthrough, fixed fee €2,400, delivered in three weeks from signed scope."
contentSections.question: Which quote can this population's practitioner actually stand behind through a variable-capacity three weeks?

options.label: Quote B — it prices the deliverable and calendar time, not the hours
Quote A — the hourly range is more honest about the real effort involved
Neither — both should just quote a day rate instead

feedback.quote-b: Correct. Quote B commits to a defined sample, a named test matrix, a specific set of deliverables, and a calendar deadline — every part of it is something the practitioner controls by planning, not by how many hours a given day allows. If week two is a flare, the plan absorbs it inside the buffer; the client never sees a broken promise, because no promise about hours was ever made.
feedback.quote-a: This reads as more transparent and is actually more fragile. "30-40 hours" is an estimate of effort, and effort is exactly the variable this population cannot promise in advance. If the real week takes 55 hours to get the same report out, the practitioner either works through a flare to protect the number or has an uncomfortable hours conversation mid-engagement — neither of which the fixed-fee version ever has to have.
feedback.neither: A day rate has the same shape as an hourly rate: it's still a promise about how many units of a specific day the practitioner will produce, and the whole premise of this lesson is that promising specific days in advance is the promise this population cannot reliably keep. Pricing the deliverable sidesteps the problem instead of renaming it.

contentSections.concept: Fixed-fee-by-deliverable isn't a pricing preference — it's a structural fit for variable capacity. It moves the risk of a slow day onto the practitioner's own schedule (where a buffer week can absorb it) instead of onto a promise made directly to the client (where a slow day becomes a broken commitment).

contentSections.scenario: You're about to reply to Marijke. Some phrases in a draft reply are the marks of a real scope statement. Others sound professional but commit to nothing, or commit to something you can't control.
contentSections.question: Select every phrase that belongs in a scope reply that protects both the engagement and your own capacity.

items.label: "The audit will cover these 10 pages, listed by template: ..."
"Tested against WCAG 2.1 AA using NVDA, VoiceOver, keyboard-only, and 200% zoom"
"Delivered within three weeks of the signed scope"
"I reply to email within two business days; calls are by appointment"
"I'll put in 35–40 hours over the next two weeks"
"Reach out any time, I'll get back to you as soon as I can"

explanation.named-sample: Belongs in the reply. A named page list is the thing both sides can point back to later if the site turns out to have more templates than either of you thought.
explanation.named-matrix: Belongs in the reply. It tells the client exactly what "tested" means, so a later "but what about Firefox" has a documented answer instead of becoming a free addition.
explanation.calendar-deadline: Belongs in the reply. A date is something the practitioner controls through planning; it makes no claim about which specific days the work happens on.
explanation.response-sla: Belongs in the reply. It sets an expectation the practitioner can hold on any week, because it describes response time, not availability or hours worked.
explanation.hours-promise: Doesn't belong. It commits to something outside the practitioner's control — how much a given week's capacity allows — and turns a bad week into an apparent broken promise rather than what it actually is.
explanation.always-on: Doesn't belong, for the same reason as the hours promise, phrased as a courtesy instead of a number. It sounds generous and commits to being reachable on days the practitioner may not have the capacity to be.

contentSections.synthesis: The four that belong all describe something the practitioner decides in advance and controls through planning: the sample, the matrix, the date, the response window. The two that don't belong both describe something a specific day decides instead — hours worked, or availability that day — which is exactly the variable this population can't promise in advance without risking a broken commitment on a bad week.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in the order that turns Marijke's vague email into a signed, honest scope.
steps: Ask clarifying questions: which storefronts/languages, any existing findings, what triggered the letter
Propose a representative page sample and confirm it covers every template that matters to the client
Name the test matrix: standard, success criteria level, AT/browser combinations
List deliverables separately, including whether a walkthrough call is included or billed separately
State a calendar timeline with a built-in buffer week, not an hours estimate
State a response-time expectation instead of an availability promise
Send the whole thing as a written scope document for sign-off before any testing starts
contentSections.explanation: The order matters because each step narrows a decision the next step depends on. You can't propose a sample before you know which storefronts are in scope, and a timeline promised before the sample is agreed is a guess wearing a date. The step most often skipped is the last one: doing the scoping conversation well and then starting work on a verbal understanding. Testing starts on a shared written document, or the first disagreement about what was agreed has no anchor to settle it — for either side.

contentSections.body: A vague request becomes a real engagement the moment it has a named page sample, a named test matrix, a deliverable list, and a calendar timeline with a buffer — priced by the deliverable, not by hours you cannot promise in advance. That document is what protects the engagement from a bad week later, because it never asked you to promise which days would be good ones.

title: Running the Audit Without Blowing the Scope
description: Execute the Havenmark audit against the plan you scoped, hold the deadline through a flare week, and answer a client who quietly adds three more page templates mid-engagement.

learningObjectives.text: Execute an audit systematically against an agreed test matrix, capturing evidence as findings are made
Distinguish a legitimate change of scope from silent scope creep, and respond to each without over-disclosing personal capacity

contentSections.body:
Nine days into the Havenmark audit, two things land on the same afternoon. First, a Slack message from Marijke: "Quick one — could you also check our new loyalty sign-up page, and can you confirm the checkout works the same for our German storefront as the rest-of-EU one? We didn't realise those ran different code." Second, your own body: the flat, wrung-out morning that means today is not a testing day, five days out from a deadline you set with a buffer week you're about to need.

Neither of these is a crisis on its own. Handled badly, together they are exactly how engagements go wrong — either you silently absorb two more templates into a fee that was priced for ten pages, or you push through a flare to protect a date, and either one costs you something the client never sees and never has to account for.

Running the audit itself is mostly a discipline problem, not a skill problem — the WCAG knowledge and AT fluency came from earlier domains in this track. What running it *well* adds is two habits that make everything after this lesson easier.

**Capture evidence as you find it, not at write-up time.** For every finding: the exact page and component, the exact WCAG success criterion, the exact words a screen reader announced or the exact keyboard behaviour observed, and a screenshot or short recording. "The checkout error message isn't announced to screen readers" is a claim. "On the payment step, submitting with an invalid card number leaves focus on the Pay button; NVDA announces nothing; the error text appears visually above the field but has no programmatic association to it — fails WCAG 2.1 SC 3.3.1 and 4.1.3" is evidence. Write findings in the second form the moment you make them, while the exact announcement is still in front of you, not from memory two weeks later when you're drafting the report.

**Work async-first, and say so.** A daily check-in call is a fixed cost you commit to whether or not that day has the capacity for a live conversation — and live conversation, for this population, often costs more than the same information delivered in writing. A single written weekly status update — pages tested, findings so far by severity, anything blocking — gives the client more real information than a daily call while costing you nothing on the days a call would have been expensive. It also creates a paper trail that the change-order conversation below leans on directly.

contentSections.scenario: Marijke's message adds two things: a new page (loyalty sign-up) and a claim you hadn't scoped for (a second checkout code path for Germany).
contentSections.question: Before reading on: what's the right first move?

options.label: Just test both — it's a small addition and you don't want to seem difficult
Say no — it's out of scope, full stop
Name it as a change to the scope, and say what it does to timeline and fee, before doing any of the new work

contentSections.revealBody: Naming it and pricing it before doing any of the work. Both of the other two responses hand something away — silently absorbing it gives away time you didn't price, refusing outright risks a relationship over a request that may well be reasonable. Naming it treats the new request exactly the way the original scope was built: as something both sides agree to in writing before it becomes work.

contentSections.body:
**Scope creep and a legitimate change request look identical in the moment — a client asking for more than what was agreed.** The difference is entirely in how you respond, not in how the request arrived.

Silently absorbing it is the most common failure, because it feels like good service. It isn't — it trains the client that the scope document was a suggestion, and it spends buffer time that was there to protect the *agreed* deliverable, not to fund new ones.

Refusing flatly is the second failure, rarer but sharper. "That's out of scope" with nothing else offered reads as inflexibility over something that, from the client's side, looked like a small ask — and it burns trust for no gain, since the honest answer usually isn't no.

The move that protects both sides: **name it as a change, price the impact, and let the client decide.** "Both are reasonable additions — the loyalty page adds roughly a day, and confirming a second checkout code path for Germany means re-running the full matrix on that path, which adds about three. That pushes delivery from the 24th to the 28th, or I can hold the 24th for the original ten pages and quote these two separately for next week. Which do you want?" This costs the client nothing they didn't already agree they might spend, and it costs you nothing you didn't already put a price on. Notice what it doesn't include: no mention of the flare, no apology for having a body that has bad days, no explanation owed for why a small-sounding request needs a real answer. The scope document is doing the work a health disclosure would otherwise be asked to do.

contentSections.scenario: Marijke replies to the change-order message: "Oh, I didn't realise it'd be that much extra work, let's just push the deadline to the 28th for all of it."
contentSections.question: What made this conversation go well, structurally?

options.label: The new work was priced and its timeline impact stated before either side agreed to anything
Marijke happened to be a reasonable client — a harder client would have needed a different approach entirely
The original buffer week absorbed the extra work, so nothing needed to change

feedback.priced-before-agreed: Correct. The reason this stayed simple is that the practitioner never did any of the new work before naming its cost. Whether Marijke turned out to be reasonable or difficult, the structure of the response — name it, price it, let the client choose — was the same, and it's the structure that did the protecting, not her personality.
feedback.client-was-reasonable: This gives the outcome credit that belongs to the process. A client who pushed back harder — "can't you just fit it in" — would meet the same priced options and the same choice; nothing about the response depended on Marijke being easy to work with. Betting an engagement's protection on the client being reasonable is exactly the bet this response was designed not to need.
feedback.buffer-absorbed-it: The buffer week was built to protect the *agreed* ten-page deliverable against a slow week, not to fund two new pages and a second checkout path for free. Using it for new scope means the original deliverable now has no buffer left — which is precisely the silent-absorption failure this lesson is warning against, just one step removed.

contentSections.concept: A change-order response protects the engagement by being priced and named *before* any new work happens, independent of how the specific client reacts to it. The habit generalises past this one message: any addition, from any client, on any week, gets the same treatment — named, priced, decided — before it becomes hours you can't get back.

contentSections.code:
Weekly status update, as drafted:

"Hi Marijke — great progress this week! Tested homepage, category, and product pages, all going smoothly. A few findings so far but nothing major. Should have everything wrapped up well ahead of schedule, might even come in early. Let me know if you want to hop on a call to go through it, happy to chat whenever works for you!"
contentSections.question: What's the real flaw in this update, given the practitioner is five days from deadline with two flare days already behind them and checkout, cart, and account still untested?

options.label: It overstates progress and offers unlimited availability, spending the only buffer that protects the deadline
The tone is too casual for a compliance-related engagement
It should list the specific findings so far, not just say "a few"

feedback.overpromises-buffer: Correct. "Ahead of schedule" and "happy to chat whenever" are both promises the practitioner cannot verify from where they're actually standing — three untested pages, two lost days, five left. If the remaining testing runs into another rough day, this update makes the deadline someone's broken promise instead of a plan working exactly as buffered. "Whenever works for you" also reopens the availability commitment the response-time SLA from the scoping conversation was built to close.
feedback.too-informal: Tone isn't the problem here — a friendly, plain-language update is a genuine strength with a client like Marijke. The flaw is what the friendly tone is saying, not how it's saying it.
feedback.no-findings-detail: A weekly summary doesn't need finding-level detail — that's what the final report is for, and re-litigating findings in a status update invites premature pushback before the evidence is fully assembled. The real problem is the update's claims about pace and availability, not its level of technical detail.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A status update's job is to report reality accurately enough that nobody downstream — including future you — has to absorb the gap between what it said and what actually happened. "Homepage through product pages tested and on track; checkout, cart, and account remain, still targeting the 24th" tells the truth and holds the same deadline without spending anything that hasn't been earned yet.

contentSections.scenario: Partway through a flare week, deciding what to do with the day in front of you.
contentSections.question: Select every signal that this is a day to protect by working the plan differently, rather than a day to push through as normal.

items.label: You can't hold focus on one page's markup for more than a few minutes without losing the thread
Physical symptoms are actively worse than your baseline testing days
You're still inside the buffer week you built into the timeline
You'd honestly rather be doing something else today
The client sent a message today, which feels like it needs an instant reply
You've logged fewer hours this week than you estimated when you priced the job

explanation.cant-hold-focus: A real signal. Accessibility testing needs sustained attention to what's actually being announced versus what the report should say happened — testing through this state produces findings that need re-checking later, which costs more time than stopping does.
explanation.symptom-flare: A real signal, and the most direct one. This is the exact situation the buffer week and the fixed-fee-by-deliverable pricing from the previous lesson exist for.
explanation.still-in-buffer: A real signal — and the reassuring kind. If the buffer hasn't been spent yet, this is a day it was built to absorb, not a crisis. Checking this before reacting to the other two is often what turns panic into a plan.
explanation.dont-feel-like-it: Not a signal specific to this — everyone has days like this regardless of health status, and treating ordinary reluctance as a capacity signal erodes the credibility of the real ones.
explanation.client-messaged: Not a signal that today needs to change — it's a signal that a message exists. The response-time SLA from the scoping conversation already answered how fast it needs a reply, and that answer doesn't change because today happens to be a harder day.
explanation.behind-on-hours: Not a signal, because there was never an hours target to be behind on — the whole point of pricing by deliverable was to make hours-per-week an irrelevant number. Checking it re-introduces exactly the metric the pricing structure was built to remove.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of these describe the actual state of the work or the body doing it. The other three describe feelings about the work that have nothing to do with capacity, and treating them as capacity signals either erodes trust in real ones or reopens a commitment (an hours target, an instant-reply expectation) that the earlier scoping work deliberately closed.

contentSections.body: Running the audit is capturing evidence at the moment you find it and communicating in writing, on a cadence you can hold on any week. Scope creep is handled the same way the original scope was built: name it, price it, let the client decide, before any of the new work happens. None of it requires disclosing why a given day is a hard one — the plan you built in the previous lesson is what's doing that job.

title: The Report, the Walkthrough, and the Client Who Pushes Back
description: Deliver the Havenmark audit report, run the findings walkthrough, and hold your severity ratings when the engineering lead argues half of them down.

learningObjectives.text: Structure an audit report and walkthrough meeting so findings can be defended with evidence rather than opinion
Distinguish a legitimate scope question from an attempt to erode findings, and respond to cost, timeline, and severity pushback accordingly

contentSections.body:
The findings walkthrough is thirty minutes in. Havenmark's engineering lead, Bram, has been quiet through most of it, then stops you on finding #4: checkout's card-error message rated Critical. "I want to push back on this one," he says. "Screen reader users are maybe two percent of our traffic, if that. Calling this Critical next to the cart-total bug feels disproportionate — can we call it Moderate?"

This is the moment the rest of the engagement was built for. Everything from the scope document to the evidence you captured mid-audit either holds here or it doesn't — and how you answer decides whether the report you deliver is the report Havenmark actually acts on.

**The report and the walkthrough are built to make this moment easy, not to react well in it.**

A report structured for defense leads with an executive summary a non-technical stakeholder reads in five minutes, then groups findings by *severity*, not by page — Critical findings first, regardless of where in the site they sit, because that's the order the client should act in, not the order a crawler found them in. Every individual finding carries four things, always in the same order: the evidence (what was actually observed, in the words captured during testing), the WCAG success criterion it fails, the concrete user impact in plain language, and remediation guidance specific enough for a developer to act on without a follow-up call. A finding built this way doesn't need you in the room to be convincing — the evidence argues for itself.

The walkthrough meeting itself is worth structuring deliberately, for the same sustainability reasons as the async-first work in the previous lesson: send the agenda and the report itself in advance, so nobody is reading findings for the first time live; offer a recording in place of a live call where the client will accept it, since a live meeting costs more than the same information delivered any other way; and when a live meeting does happen, know before you walk in which findings are likely to draw pushback, because you wrote the report and you know which ones rest on judgment calls rather than a clear-cut SC violation.

contentSections.scenario: Bram's argument is about traffic percentage, not about the evidence in finding #4.
contentSections.question: Before reading on: what's the strongest first move in response?

options.label: Point back to the severity rubric the scope agreed to, and show what it says about this finding's actual criteria
Meet him halfway — agree to downgrade to a rating between Critical and Moderate
Counter with a different traffic or legal statistic that argues the two percent number is wrong

contentSections.revealBody: Anchoring to the rubric. Bram isn't wrong that traffic percentage is a real business consideration — he's applying a criterion that was never part of how severity gets decided in this engagement. The rubric, agreed before any testing started, is the thing both sides already committed to using. Pointing back to it isn't stonewalling; it's the fastest way to show the disagreement is about which yardstick applies, not about whose opinion is stronger.

contentSections.body:
**Severity ratings hold up under pushback when they were never a matter of opinion to begin with.** A severity rubric — agreed in the original scope, the same way the page sample and test matrix were — defines each level by *what the finding does to a user's ability to complete a task*, independent of how many users hit it: Critical blocks task completion entirely for a user of that AT with no workaround; Serious creates a significant barrier with a difficult or non-obvious workaround; Moderate creates friction but the task remains completable; Minor is a deviation from best practice with no meaningful task impact. Checkout's card-error message is Critical under that definition specifically because a screen reader user who submits an invalid card has no way to discover why the payment failed — not because of how many people that happens to. Traffic percentage answers a different, legitimate question — *how much business impact does fixing this have* — and belongs in the prioritisation conversation, not in the severity rating itself.

**Cost and timeline pushback get a different, calmer answer: the signed scope document.** "The fee and delivery date were set against the ten-page sample and matrix we agreed in writing before testing started — if there's a change to that scope, I'm glad to price it the way we did the loyalty page addition" reopens nothing that wasn't already closed, and it does it without relitigating the whole engagement live in the room.

**And when a question genuinely needs more thought than the room allows** — which, on a day the live meeting itself is already costing you more than a written exchange would — "let me confirm the specifics and follow up in writing by tomorrow" is a complete, professional answer. It is not a concession, and it is not weakness. It is the same async-first principle from the previous lesson, applied to the one moment in the engagement where a live room is hardest to avoid entirely.

contentSections.scenario:
Two versions of how the meeting could go from here:

**Response A:** "That's fair, let's call it Moderate — I don't want this to hold up the rest of the report."

**Response B:** "The rubric we agreed rates severity by task impact for the user hitting it, not by traffic share — a screen reader user submitting an invalid card gets no error at all under the current markup, which is a full block with no workaround, so it stays Critical under that definition. Traffic share is a real factor for how you prioritise the fix queue, and I'm glad to help think through that separately."
contentSections.question: Which response protects the report's credibility for whoever reads it after this meeting — the developers who have to fix it, and any future auditor who has to verify the fix?

options.label: Response B — it defends the rating on its own defined terms and offers Bram's real concern a place to go
Response A — keeping the meeting moving and the relationship warm matters more than one rating
Neither — the practitioner should have avoided rating anything Critical to prevent this conversation entirely

feedback.response-b: Correct. Response B does two things at once: it holds the rating on the exact grounds the rubric defines, and it validates that Bram's underlying concern — business impact — is real and has a legitimate place, just not inside the severity number. Nothing about it is combative; all of it is anchored to something both sides already agreed to.
feedback.response-a: This feels collaborative in the room and costs something real outside it: the next reader of this report — a developer prioritising a fix queue, or a future auditor checking whether Critical findings were resolved — now sees a Moderate rating attached to a finding that fully blocks task completion for the AT user hitting it. The report stops matching the rubric it claims to use, and every rating in it becomes negotiable rather than evidenced.
feedback.split-difference: Softening every rating in advance to avoid this conversation defeats the purpose of running the audit at all — the client is paying for an honest severity assessment, and a report that quietly avoids Critical ratings to keep meetings smooth is a report that has stopped doing its job before the meeting even happens.

contentSections.concept: A severity rating defended on its rubric survives disagreement about a different question — business priority — without changing, because the rating was never answering that question in the first place. Conceding under live pressure doesn't resolve the disagreement; it just moves the report's credibility problem to whoever reads it next.

contentSections.scenario: Not every pushback in a findings walkthrough is an attempt to erode the report. Some are legitimate scope or prioritisation questions that deserve a real answer.
contentSections.question: Select every pushback that is a legitimate question about scope or prioritisation, rather than an attempt to relitigate an already-agreed finding.

items.label: "Given our dev capacity, which three findings should we fix first?"
"Was the Belgian storefront included in the AT matrix, or just the Dutch one?"
"Can you break down what part of the fee covered the walkthrough versus the report itself?"
"Can we downgrade this from Critical to Moderate based on how few users it affects?"
"Since you already found this on one product page, can you just skip checking whether it's on the others?"
"Our last agency never flagged this as Critical, so maybe your bar is too strict"

explanation.priority-order: Legitimate. This asks the report to do the job the prioritisation section exists for, and it's a genuinely useful conversation to have — business constraints are real and belong in sequencing the fix queue.
explanation.matrix-boundary: Legitimate. A question about what was actually tested is a scope question with a factual answer, pointing straight back to the agreed test matrix. Answering it plainly reinforces the matrix rather than threatening it.
explanation.cost-breakdown: Legitimate. Asking what a fee covered is a reasonable billing question, and the original scope document already has the answer on hand.
explanation.downgrade-rubric: Not legitimate as asked. It's applying a criterion — traffic share — the rubric never used to set severity, functionally asking to change what "Critical" means partway through the engagement.
explanation.reopen-sample: Not legitimate. Sampling logic said a finding on one template applies to every page using that template — the client is asking to reverse the reasoning that made the audit efficient in the first place, in the direction that produces a cleaner-looking report rather than a more accurate one.
explanation.discount-severity: Not legitimate as an argument, though worth noting for a different reason: it says something true and uncomfortable about the previous vendor's rigor, not something that should move this report's rubric.

contentSections.synthesis: The legitimate three all ask questions the scope document or rubric already has an answer to, and answering them plainly makes the report more useful, not weaker. The other three all ask, in different words, for a rating or a fact to move for a reason the agreed criteria never included — which is the real test for whether pushback needs an evidence-based hold or a straightforward answer.

contentSections.question: Bram's pushback lands live, mid-meeting, on a day the meeting itself is already costing more than usual. Put the response steps in order.
steps: Restate what the pushback is actually asking — a rubric question or a scope question
Answer directly from the rubric or the signed scope document, out loud
Name the legitimate concern underneath it and where it does belong (prioritisation, billing, matrix boundary)
If it needs more than the room allows right now, say so and commit to a written follow-up by a specific time
Send that follow-up in writing, even when the live answer already settled it
contentSections.explanation: Restating the question before answering it does real work: it slows a live, possibly costly moment down to one clear thing to respond to, instead of an open-ended debate. Answering from a document instead of from memory or improvisation is what makes the answer hold up later, for anyone reading the report who wasn't in the room. The step people skip under live pressure is the last one — sending a written follow-up even when the meeting already resolved it. That written trail is what the next disagreement, if there is one, gets settled against.

contentSections.body: A report built with evidence, a rubric, and remediation guidance in every finding defends itself before the meeting starts. In the room, severity holds against a rubric; cost and timeline hold against the signed scope; and "let me follow up in writing" is a complete answer, not a retreat — especially on the day a live room costs more than it usually does.

title: The Portfolio Artefact: Turning the Engagement into Evidence
description: Package the completed Havenmark engagement into a portfolio case study an employer can actually read — what to anonymise, how to describe your own contribution truthfully, and the capstone brief, rubric, and worked exemplar for this domain's deliverable.

learningObjectives.text: Select what to include, anonymise, and omit when converting a completed client engagement into a portfolio artefact
Produce a portfolio case study of a completed audit engagement that meets a published rubric, describing personal contribution truthfully

contentSections.body: A hiring manager screening candidates for a contract accessibility QA role has eleven portfolios open in browser tabs and about thirty seconds for each one before deciding whether to keep reading. She is not reading your résumé first — she is opening the one artefact you linked and checking, in order: is this a real finding from a real test, or a WCAG checklist restated in prose; can I tell what this person actually did versus what a team did; and does a single claim in here sound inflated. The Havenmark engagement you just ran is real work. This lesson is about making sure the thirty-second read of it lands.

**What belongs in the case study** is a small, honest slice of what you just did, not a re-narration of the entire engagement: the scope you worked from (sample, matrix, deliverables — this shows planning, not just testing), one or two representative findings shown in full (evidence, WCAG SC, user impact, remediation guidance — this is the actual work product a reviewer wants to see), one before/after remediation example if you have one, and a short methodology paragraph describing how you tested, not just what standard you tested against.

**What has to be anonymised, and how.** The client's name and any identifying detail (exact revenue, exact traffic numbers, internal ticket or system IDs, any named employee other than a role like "the engineering lead") comes out — not blurred, replaced: "a mid-size EU home-and-lifestyle retailer" carries exactly as much useful information as "Havenmark" does for a hiring manager evaluating your skill, and it respects a confidentiality expectation most client contracts state explicitly even when they don't have to. Screenshots get the same treatment: crop or redact anything that names the client, and say plainly in a caption that it has been redacted — an unexplained crop reads as sloppy; a labelled one reads as careful.

**Describing your own contribution truthfully is the part most portfolios get wrong**, usually toward overstatement. If you tested a defined ten-page sample, say sample, not "audited the entire platform." If you delivered findings and remediation guidance but didn't write or ship the fix, say that — "I identified and prioritised the following issues; the development team implemented the fix shown" is a complete, honest, and still impressive sentence. If you worked solo, say solo; if you worked as part of a team, say what your specific piece was. None of this makes the work sound smaller. A hiring manager who has read enough inflated portfolios recognises specific, bounded claims as the mark of someone who can be trusted to report a real finding accurately later — which is, after all, the actual job.

contentSections.scenario: Hiring managers screening accessibility portfolios were asked what single thing most often makes them stop reading and move to the next tab.
contentSections.question: Before reading on: what's the most common disqualifier?

options.label: A claim that's vague or overstated relative to what's actually shown as evidence
Too few findings shown — fewer than five or six examples
No remediation code included, only findings

contentSections.revealBody: A vague or overstated claim, almost every time. "Led a comprehensive accessibility overhaul" next to one finding with no evidence attached reads as a claim with nothing behind it, and it costs more trust than showing two well-evidenced findings and being specific about scope ever does. Volume and remediation code are secondary — a hiring manager can usually tell within one paragraph whether the claims match the evidence, and that's the test the rest of the portfolio doesn't get a chance to pass if it fails.

contentSections.body: **This domain's portfolio artefact is the case study itself — here is the brief, the rubric, and a worked exemplar, so you can produce a real one from this lesson alone.**

**The brief.** Produce a one-to-two page portfolio case study of a completed accessibility audit engagement (the Havenmark engagement from this domain, or a real engagement of your own if you have one). It must include: (1) an anonymised scope summary — sample, matrix, deliverables, timeline; (2) two to three representative findings in full, each with evidence, WCAG success criterion, user impact, and remediation guidance; (3) a short methodology paragraph; (4) a one-paragraph, specific, honest description of your own contribution to the work. The whole piece must be readable by a non-specialist hiring manager in under three minutes.

**The rubric.** Five dimensions, each rated Pass or Excellent — a submission needs Pass on all five to count as complete.

**Scope clarity** — *Pass:* the sample, matrix, and deliverables are stated and specific. *Excellent:* the scope explains, in one sentence, *why* that sample is representative (e.g. one instance per interaction pattern), showing the reasoning, not just the list.

**Evidence quality** — *Pass:* each finding names the exact page, component, WCAG SC, and observed AT behaviour. *Excellent:* the exact wording of what the AT actually announced or did is quoted, distinguishing a real test from a restated checklist.

**Remediation guidance** — *Pass:* each finding includes guidance specific enough for a developer to act on. *Excellent:* guidance names the specific fix (e.g. the exact markup or attribute change) rather than a general principle like "add appropriate ARIA."

**Anonymisation and truthful attribution** — *Pass:* no identifying client detail remains, and the contribution paragraph states what the candidate personally did. *Excellent:* the contribution paragraph is specific enough to distinguish exactly what was tested/written/delivered from what a team or the client's own developers did, with no phrase that could be read as claiming more.

**Sustainability framing** — *Pass:* the methodology paragraph doesn't claim or imply an unsustainable pace (e.g. no "delivered overnight" or "available 24/7"). *Excellent:* the methodology paragraph explicitly and matter-of-factly names a working pattern — async-first communication, fixed-fee-by-deliverable, calendar-based timeline — as a deliberate professional choice, not an apology.

**Worked exemplar**, meeting every dimension at Excellent:

---

**Accessibility Audit — EU Retail Client, Home & Lifestyle Sector**

*Scope:* A ten-page representative sample was selected to cover every distinct interaction pattern on the client's webshop rather than every URL — homepage, category listing, product detail, search (including zero-results), cart, three checkout steps, account/login, and one content form — on the reasoning that a finding on a shared template applies to every page using it. Tested against WCAG 2.1 AA using NVDA + Chrome, VoiceOver + Safari, keyboard-only navigation, and 200% zoom, delivered as a severity-rated report and a recorded findings walkthrough within a three-week fixed-fee engagement.

*Finding 1 — Critical.* Checkout, payment step. Submitting an invalid card number leaves focus on the Pay button; NVDA announces nothing further. The error text renders visually above the card field but has no `aria-describedby` or other programmatic association to it. Fails WCAG 2.1 SC 3.3.1 (Error Identification) and 4.1.3 (Status Messages). A screen reader user has no way to discover the payment failed or why — a full block with no workaround. *Remediation:* add `role="alert"` to the error container so it is announced on render, and add `aria-describedby` on the card input pointing at the error element's id, so the association survives even if the user tabs back to the field directly.

*Finding 2 — Serious.* Product listing page, filter panel. Filter checkboxes are custom-built `<div>` elements styled to look like checkboxes; they respond to click but not to keyboard activation, and carry no `role` or `aria-checked`. Fails WCAG 2.1 SC 2.1.1 (Keyboard) and 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value). A keyboard-only user can tab to each filter but cannot activate any of them — a significant barrier with no in-page workaround, though the equivalent unfiltered results remain browsable. *Remediation:* replace the custom `<div>` with a native `<input type="checkbox">` wrapped in a `<label>`, which restores keyboard activation and correct role/state reporting with no JavaScript required.

*Methodology:* Findings were tested and evidenced individually as they were found — exact AT announcements recorded at the time of testing rather than reconstructed at write-up — then organised by severity for the report rather than by page order, so the client's engineering team could act on the highest-impact issues first. Client communication ran async-first: a written weekly status update in place of daily calls, with live discussion reserved for the scheduled findings walkthrough. This is a deliberate way of working, not a workaround — it keeps the engagement's pace independent of any single day's variable capacity, while still meeting every deadline in the signed scope.

*My contribution:* I scoped, tested, and wrote this audit independently as the sole practitioner on the engagement — the client's own development team implemented the remediation shown above; I reviewed the shipped fix for finding 1 against the original success criterion to confirm it resolved the issue.

---

Notice what the exemplar never does: it never names the client, never states a traffic or revenue number, never claims to have written or shipped code it didn't write or ship, and never apologises for or explains the async-first working pattern — it states it as a professional choice, because that is what it is.

contentSections.scenario: Draft sentences from different candidates' contribution paragraphs, describing the same kind of solo audit engagement.
contentSections.question: Select every sentence that describes contribution honestly and specifically enough to pass the rubric's attribution dimension.

items.label: "I scoped, tested, and wrote this audit independently as the sole practitioner; the client's team implemented the fixes shown."
"I was one of three testers on this engagement; my assigned pages were checkout and account, and the findings shown here are from that portion."
"I identified and prioritised these issues and wrote the remediation guidance; I did not implement the code changes."
"I led a comprehensive accessibility overhaul of the client's e-commerce platform."
"We fixed the accessibility issues across the site."
"I audited the entire platform and certified it WCAG 2.1 AA compliant."

explanation.solo-scoped-tested: Passes. It states the role (sole practitioner), the actual verbs (scoped, tested, wrote), and correctly attributes the implementation to the client's own team — a reader knows exactly what this person did and did not do.
explanation.team-my-part: Passes. On a team engagement, naming the specific slice that was personally handled is what makes the claim checkable and fair to the other two testers' work.
explanation.reviewed-not-shipped: Passes. This is the honest version of the most common gap in this kind of engagement — finding issues versus fixing them — stated plainly instead of blurred.
explanation.led-overhaul: Doesn't pass. "Led" implies authority over a team or process that a solo fixed-fee engagement never had, and "comprehensive overhaul" overstates a ten-page sample into the whole platform.
explanation.we-fixed: Doesn't pass, on two counts: "we" on a solo engagement invents collaborators, and "fixed" claims implementation work that, in the exemplar's actual engagement, belonged to the client's own developers.
explanation.audited-entire: Doesn't pass, and the word "certified" adds a second problem: a WCAG audit finds and rates conformance issues against a sample — it isn't a certification, and no accessibility audit, however thorough, can honestly claim to guarantee compliance the way that word implies.

contentSections.synthesis: The three that pass all use verbs that match something the practitioner actually did, scoped to something actually true — sole practitioner, team member on a defined slice, findings-not-fixes. The three that fail all borrow authority, scope, or outcomes — leading, fixing, certifying — that the engagement as described never actually had.

contentSections.body: A portfolio artefact earns thirty seconds of trust the same way a defended finding earns a client's: specific evidence, a stated rubric, and a contribution described in verbs that match what actually happened. The engagement you just ran through this domain — scoped, executed, delivered, defended — is the raw material. This lesson's brief, rubric, and exemplar are what turn it into something an employer can verify rather than just take your word for.
